explain.say: Those crusty orange, grey or green patches on rocks, walls and tree bark are lichens. A lichen is not one living thing but a partnership between a fungus and a tiny alga or cyanobacterium.

faq.q: How do the fungus and alga help each other?
faq.a: The alga makes sugar from sunlight and feeds the fungus. The fungus gives the alga a safe, damp home, shade from strong light and minerals. Together they live where neither could alone.

faq.q: How do lichens grow on bare rock?
faq.a: They need no soil. They get water from rain, dew and fog, minerals from dust and rock, and food from their alga. Root-like threads anchor them, and their acids slowly break the rock down.
Very slowly; many grow only about a millimetre a year. Some are thought to be thousands of years old, and scientists use lichen size to estimate how long rocks have been exposed.

faq.q: Why are lichens a sign of clean air?
faq.a: Lichens soak up everything from rain and air, so many kinds are harmed by pollution such as sulphur dioxide. Lots of different lichens on trees usually means clean air.
Yes. Reindeer and caribou survive Arctic winters on reindeer lichen, digging it out from under the snow. Some birds also use lichen to build their nests.

facts: Simon Schwendener proposed in 1867 that a lichen is a partnership between a fungus and an alga.
Many lichens grow only about a millimetre a year.
Reindeer lichen is a main winter food for reindeer and caribou.
